data.name: FINAL FANTASY XII THE ZODIAC AGE
data.detailed_description:
FINAL FANTASY XII THE ZODIAC AGE - This revered classic returns, now fully remastered for the first time for PC, featuring all new and enhanced gameplay.

RETURN TO THE WORLD OF IVALICE
Enter an era of war within the world of Ivalice. The small kingdom of Dalmasca, conquered by the Archadian Empire, is left in ruin and uncertainty. Princess Ashe, the one and only heir to the throne, devotes herself to the resistance to liberate her country.

Vaan, a young man who lost his family in the war, dreams of flying freely in the skies. In a fight for freedom and fallen royalty, join these unlikely allies and their companions as they embark on a heroic adventure to free their homeland.

Players both returning and new to the game will be immersed in a grand adventure that spans the world of Ivalice in an entirely fresh and improved experience.

KEY FEATURES:
  • New Zodiac Job system with improved battle mechanics.
  • Newly implemented trophies.
  • True 7.1 Surround sound including HD voicing and fully remastered music.
  • Choose between original in-game BGM, new re-orchestrated BGM and original soundtrack.
  • Endless adventure including hunts, battles and mini-games.
  • 60 FPS - Ivalice will look even more spectacular running at 60FPS
  • Compatible with 21:9 ultra wide monitors
  • New Game Plus and New Game Minus
  • Maximized License Points and Gil
  • Full controller support, Steam Trading Cards and more!

reviews.review:
[i]"You've changed, Vaan."[/i]

No, for fuck's sake, Penelo. Not nearly enough.

Final Fantasy XII is one of the finest games in the series, which makes its insistence on placing Vaan front and center all the more frustrating.

The [i]Star Wars[/i] comparisons are hard to miss: empires, rebellions, political intrigue, and a young man dreaming of adventure. But while Luke Skywalker grows from a restless farm boy into someone shaped by his experiences, failures, and choices, Vaan spends much of his journey standing beside more compelling characters. He sees the world change without convincing us that he has changed with it.

Of course, FFXII doesn't need another Luke Skywalker. Its ensemble cast is its greatest narrative strength. Ashe struggles with revenge and responsibility, Basch with honor and disgrace, and Balthier with a past he cannot escape. Their personal conflicts give the game's political story its weight.

The story's ambition goes further than its characters. What begins as a struggle over Dalmasca becomes a question of who has the right to decide the course of history, whether kings, empires, or powers claiming to stand above humanity. Ashe's choices give that conflict real stakes: revenge may feel justified, but the people she hopes to save could pay the price.

Vaan has a legitimate place among them. As a war orphan, he represents ordinary people caught between powerful nations, and his shared grief with Ashe gives him some emotional significance. Yet the game rarely develops his own journey beyond naïveté and comic interruptions. He doesn't need to save Ivalice. He needs a personal story that makes his prominence feel justified.

The group is the real protagonist, but Vaan remains its face.

Fortunately, Final Fantasy XII has far more to offer than its uneven character development.

Ivalice is one of Final Fantasy's most fascinating settings. Having known this world since [i]Final Fantasy Tactics[/i], returning to its cities and landscapes never gets old. Rabanastre, Bhujerba, and Archades feel inhabited rather than built merely to move the party between objectives. Crowded streets, different peoples, and the contrast between great cities and remote villages make the world feel larger than the party's mission. The attention to architecture and everyday details remains impressive even today.

The visuals have aged remarkably well, and the soundtrack deserves just as much praise. I still listen to Final Fantasy XII's [i]Piano Collections[/i] while studying or working, years after my first playthrough.

But it's the game's bones that make it so replayable. Strip away the spectacle, and FFXII would still be a compelling RPG. Gambits let you set conditional behaviors for your party, turning combat into an exercise in planning and experimentation. There is something immensely satisfying about watching a carefully constructed setup work, and something educational about watching it fail spectacularly.

The Zodiac Age's job combinations open up different party builds, while Hunts, rare monsters, equipment, loot, and exploration all feed into one another. A quick errand becomes a detour, an unexpected encounter, another piece of gear to chase. There is pleasure in remembering which enemies drop what, how to prepare for a dangerous fight, and where an unfamiliar road might lead. The systems don't just coexist; they give each other purpose.

Not everything works equally well. Some secrets are needlessly obscure, while certain activities turn exploration into tedious housekeeping. Even a game built around freedom can occasionally mistake repetition for meaningful content.

Those frustrations are real, but they hardly define Final Fantasy XII. Few RPGs make building a party, hunting for equipment, and wandering off the main road feel so much like parts of the same adventure.

Vaan's journey may leave something to be desired. The journey through Ivalice does not.

[b]Rating:[/b] 9 Skulls and a Femur - 💀💀💀💀💀💀💀💀💀

[b]Cause of Death:[/b] Still waiting for Vaan to change.
